answer.exemplar: The two claims protect different things, which is why both sound like the rule of law to their authors. The first treats the rule of law as a limit on the state: emergency powers must be bounded by law that the government itself cannot suspend at will, and a claim to that effect is misleading when officials retain unchecked discretion or when the proclamation is never reviewed. The second treats it as government by consent: so long as a legislature elected and accountable to voters passes the law by the agreed procedure, the law has the consent it needs, and insisting on judicial limits on it undercuts the consent the rule of law is meant to guarantee. Neither version is the whole phrase, so the test to apply is what the speaker wants protected: the constitution against the government, or the enacted decision against anyone who disputes it.

questions.explanation: This item tests the idea that the phrase covers competing conceptions, and that the argument only moves once you ask what is being protected. A rights-protective version insists that legal limits bind the state even under pressure, while a consent-based version insists that properly enacted law is itself legitimate. Each claim misleads when it is presented as the only meaning: the first when the supposed limit has no review behind it, the second when consent is assumed for a law citizens had no real chance to influence.
questions.hint: Ask what each side is trying to protect, and from whom.
questions.learningObjective: compare competing conceptions of the rule of law

answer.exemplar: The two verdicts turn on the same act for opposite reasons, and the difference is which institution is entitled to have the last word. Review is defensible when the measure offends a right the constitution actually protects, when the court applies a standard the text supports, and when it supplies a reasoned correction the legislature may adopt rather than a veto it must absorb; on those conditions the court is doing the job of protecting a legal order from a temporary majority. It becomes overreach when it treats contested policy choices as rights questions, reads a silence into a constitution, or substitutes its own budget for the legislature's, because then the court is exercising power it was never given and no future government can undo it. The practical test is whether the ruling narrows the government or simply replaces it.

questions.explanation: This item tests the line between a court protecting an entrenched legal order and a court taking over ordinary political choice, which turns on legal grounding and on the effect of the ruling. A ruling that vindicates a right the constitution protects and states a workable standard is a correction a legislature can adopt; one that resolves a distributive debate or asserts a right the text never mentions has no source in law. The answer must give the test rather than pick a side by label.
questions.hint: Ask whether the ruling narrows the government or replaces it.
questions.learningObjective: distinguish defensible judicial review from overreach

answer.exemplar: The text tells you what the state has promised and which institution may enforce it; it cannot tell you whether anyone uses either. A written bill of rights is a starting point that has been met in some countries and ignored in others with the same language, and a court with real power changes nothing if it issues no reasons, hears nothing and reaches no one, because unenforceable judgments leave the conduct untouched. The evidence that would settle it is empirical: what share of judgments are published, how they are enforced against the losing party, how long cases take, whether the budget is appropriated, and whether officials who lose actually comply. Until those figures exist, the constitution describes an intention, and a claim that the rule of law is secure on the strength of the text alone mistakes a design for an outcome.

questions.explanation: This item tests the distinction between legal design and legal effect, and it should resist the temptation to treat an impressive text as proof of practice. Design elements are observable in the constitution itself: entrenched guarantees, an independent court, funding rules, published judgments. Effect is observed in behaviour: how often judgments are enforced, whether the budget is actually appropriated, how quickly contested cases are resolved, and whether the losing side complies. The gap between the two lists is what any honest assessment of that country would have to measure.
questions.hint: Separate what the text promises from what the courts actually do.
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what constitutional design cannot establish about practice

questions.explanation: Two of the three failures are about getting a result to matter: a court able to enforce its own judgments and judgments published with reasons turn decisions into something a losing party and a later judge must confront. Transparent shortlist appointment with fixed non-renewable terms addresses the third failure, the risk of political capture, by making entry and exit depend on published criteria. More judges of the same kind changes speed at best, since a judgment that cannot be enforced or inspected is not improved by a longer queue behind it.

answer.exemplar: The two changes pull in opposite directions. Halving the appeal window removes the slowest and most obviously wrong decisions from the system, which protects the quality of what finally stands, but it is the only route by which many people can challenge an error at all, so a shorter window removes their chance rather than the error. A fixed appeal fee does the same thing more sharply, since a small claim will not absorb it while a large corporate one will, which converts a right of appeal into a privilege of the wealthy. Together they make the system faster and the outcomes more reliable for parties who could afford to litigate twice, and quietly less just for everyone else; a version that keeps the window and waives the fee for small claims would capture most of the error-correction gain without the distributional cost.

questions.explanation: This item tests whether an efficiency measure and a charging rule are judged against the same goal. Speeding up appeals reduces the number of surviving errors but also the number of errors anyone can get corrected, and a fixed fee reallocates the right of appeal towards parties who can absorb it. Neither is wrong in isolation, and the evaluation has to name which values are traded, who pays in each case, and what a design would look like that kept the gain without concentrating the cost.
questions.hint: Ask who loses the chance to correct a decision under each change.
